title: The MGC Inflection Point
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Drawing on a year of partnering with schools to implement The Will to Learn, Dave Stuart Jr. names a predictable "inflection point" that hits every faculty attempting Moments of Genuine Connection (MGCs): after the initial push of printing rosters and tracking interactions, resistance sets in, sounding like "I already do this, why keep track?" and feeling like exhaustion, pressure, apathy, and anger. Borrowing Steven Pressfield's concept of Resistance from The War of Art, he reframes this dip as a normal, temporary decline that precedes further progress rather than a sign the strategy has failed. His three-part response for schools hitting this point is to surface the pushback and hard feelings directly, surface the rationale by sharing concrete positive stories, and clarify the practice itself — including a precise definition of what an MGC actually is versus what it isn't. He closes by reiterating the target cadence of two to three MGCs per class per day, acknowledging it feels onerous at first but becomes habitual with repetition.
points: Stuart names the predictable mid-implementation dip in MGC practice an "inflection point," borrowing Steven Pressfield's concept of Resistance to reframe it as expected rather than a failure signal.
His three-part school-support method — surface the pushback, surface the rationale, clarify the practice — gives leaders a repeatable protocol for coaching faculty through the dip.

His precise definition of an MGC — an intentional, other-directed interaction that communicates "I see you, I respect you, I value you" — distinguishes it from passively responding to a student-initiated comment.
He explicitly sets the bar low on individual MGC quality ("They don't need to be LONG or AMAZING or DEEP") to reduce the perfectionism that fuels resistance.
The target cadence he specifies, two to three MGCs per class per day, gives schools a concrete, trackable benchmark rather than a vague aspiration.
quotes: Here's what the resistance sounds like: I already do this. Why do I need to keep track? I don't have time to do this.
The good news is, it's an inflection point — a momentary pause in upward progress, a brief decline before another rise if you keep going.
It's an interaction with a student where you're TRYING TO COMMUNICATE that you value, know, or respect them. You have a main intention in the interaction: I see you. I respect you. I value you.
It's instead one of those moments where you go up to the kid and ask them how the game went last night. YOU thought of THEM.
They don't need to be LONG or AMAZING or DEEP. They just need to be intentional.
